content.title: About
content.content: A cream cake is a dessert composed of several layers of sponge cake soaked with syrup and a sweet cream, usually made from cream, eggs, and sugar. The cake can be decorated with fruit, chocolate, nuts, and other decorative elements.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream cakes appeared in Europe in the 17th century and quickly became popular at celebrations.
The most famous cream is the French "crème pâtissière," made from cream, eggs, and sugar.
The traditional cake sponge is often called "sponge" because it is light and airy.
In Russia, cakes like "Napoleon" and "Medovik" are popular, where the cream plays a key role.
Cakes are commonly used as symbols of celebration—from weddings to birthdays.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cream made from dairy products contains calcium, which is important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Cake provides a quick source of energy due to its carbohydrates and fats, which can be useful during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy in the cream supply vitamins B2 and B12, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Cream cakes often contain a lot of sugar, which can contribute to tooth decay and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream based on milk can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Cakes are rich in fats and carbohydrates, so they should be consumed in moderation, especially when weight control is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cream cake in slices, usually as a single piece. It pairs well with berries, fruit, ice cream, or coffee. For a lighter option, use a low‑fat cream or replace part of the cream with yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cake in the refrigerator, covered with plastic wrap, for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze individual portions in an airtight container and thaw in the refrigerator before serving.

chicken-drumstick-fried-coated-prepared-.title: Chicken drumstick, fried, coated, skinless, coating eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken drumsticks that are deep‑fried in a crispy coating are juicy inside and flavorful outside. The coating, usually made from flour, spices and sometimes breadcrumbs, is completely edible. This product is commonly served as a snack or main dish in fast‑food restaurants and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks contain more connective tissue than breast meat, which makes them especially moist after frying.
Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust while sealing in moisture.
Coatings often include paprika, garlic, onion, and black pepper for extra flavor.
In many cuisines the drumsticks are served with barbecue, honey‑mustard, or spicy chili sauces.
Chicken drumsticks are a key ingredient in dishes like paprikash, chicken stew, and many Asian stir‑fries.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Phosphorus, selenium and zinc in the meat contribute to bone health, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Ideal for low‑carb diets as they provide energy without significant carbs.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Protein and a modest amount of fat help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated and possibly trans fats, so consumption should be moderate.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: The coating often contains salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 74 °C.

items.title: Allergy to coating ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to wheat, gluten or spices used in the breading.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried coated drumsticks can be enjoyed hot as a standalone dish, served with potatoes, rice or vegetable sides. They are often paired with sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, garlic aioli or spicy chili sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked drumsticks in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a bag at –18 °C, where they retain quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-made-with-an.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg made with animal fat or meat drippings (1975)

content.title: About
content.content: A dish of eggs cooked in animal fat (such as butter, beef tallow or pork lard) or on meat drippings. In 1975 this method was common in traditional cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Animal fat gives the dish a distinctive aroma and higher caloric density.
In the 1970s, using meat drippings instead of oil was typical in rural households.
Eggs are a good source of protein, B‑vitamins and choline.
Traditionally the omelet was cooked in a cast‑iron skillet for even heat distribution.
Some regions added finely chopped meat or bacon for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them a complete protein source.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The yolk provides vitamins A, D, E, K and minerals such as iron and selenium.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: Animal fat raises the energy content of the dish, which was valuable when food supplies were limited.

items.title: Improved absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: The presence of fat enhances the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K from the eggs.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Frequent consumption of dishes cooked in animal fat may increase cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne infection
items.content: Undercooked eggs can contain Salmonella.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to eggs, experiencing reactions from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: The dish can be very calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, season with salt and pepper. Heat a skillet with a small amount of animal fat, pour in the egg mixture and cook to the desired doneness, optionally adding finely chopped meat or bacon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat with a little fresh fat to restore flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Goose, wild, roasted is the meat of wild geese that has been pre‑roasted to a golden crust. The meat has a rich flavor, firm texture, and the distinctive aroma of game birds. It is used in traditional dishes, appetizers, and as a standalone delicacy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild geese feed on a variety of plants, seeds, and small insects, giving their meat a unique taste.
In ancient cultures the wild goose was a symbol of abundance and often served at festive feasts.
Wild goose meat contains more protein and less fat than domestic goose meat.
Traditionally, wild geese were roasted over open fire, imparting a subtle smoky flavor.
In some regions the wild goose is considered a seasonal delicacy, available only during hunting season.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Goose meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with domestic goose, wild goose has less saturated fat, making it a leaner option.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Iron supports normal blood formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins source
items.content: Contains B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports the immune system.

items.title: Bird allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry, including goose.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Wild goose meat is high in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C.

items.title: Added sodium
items.content: Roasting often involves salt; those monitoring sodium intake should consider this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve roasted wild goose hot as a main course, slice thinly for sandwiches, add to salads, or use in warm appetizers. It pairs well with berry sauces, cranberry or apple chutney.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the roasted goose in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.

green-peas-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Green peas, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pods of the pea plant (Pisum sativum) harvested before the seeds fully mature. They are typically boiled in salted water without added fat, resulting in a tender, slightly sweet vegetable rich in plant protein and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are the ancestors of many modern pea varieties.
Ancient cultures used peas as a food source and for medicinal purposes.
Fresh green peas contain more vitamin C than most other legumes.
Peas can fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.
In many countries green peas are traditionally served as purees or soups.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: One cup of cooked green peas provides about 8 g of plant protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas supply folate, thiamine, and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They contain iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for blood formation, bones, and cardiovascular function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared without added oil, peas contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Peas contain purines, so people with gout should limit their intake.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas and intestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be enjoyed as a side dish, added to salads, soups, stews, purees, or used as a filling for pies. They also freeze well in portioned bags for quick reheating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked green peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags, where they keep quality for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti sauce is a ready‑to‑use tomato sauce seasoned with basil, oregano, garlic and olive oil. It is designed for quick preparation of classic Italian pasta dishes, delivering a rich aroma and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce first appeared in Italy in the 19th century as a method of preserving tomatoes.
Traditional recipes contain only tomatoes, onion, garlic and dried herbs, without added sugar.
The sauce is used not only for spaghetti but also as a base for pizza, ragù and casseroles.
In authentic Italian cooking tomatoes are simmered for at least 30 minutes to develop flavor.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sauce supplies vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared without added butter, the sauce contains little saturated fat.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Tomatoes add a modest amount of dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Commercial sauces can be high in sodium; people with hypertension should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or the spices used.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands contain preservatives such as potassium sorbate, which may cause sensitivity in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Heat the sauce in a saucepan, add cooked spaghetti and stir. It can be enriched with ground meat, seafood, vegetables or topped with grated Parmesan cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it refrigerated and use within 5 days. Discard if any off‑odor or mold appears.
